results.content: # What is worst-case execution time (WCET) analysis? WCET analysis provides the mathematical certainty that your real-time systems will meet their deadlines, even under the most demanding conditions. For tech startups and scale-ups developing embedded solutions, mastering timing analysis can mean the difference between a successful product launch and costly system failures in the field. **Worst-case execution time analysis** is a systematic approach to determining the maximum time a piece of code will take to execute under any possible conditions. Unlike average execution times, WCET analysis focuses on the absolute upper bound, providing guarantees that are essential for safety-critical applications. In real-time embedded systems, WCET analysis serves as the foundation for schedulability analysis. The analysis considers all possible execution paths, input combinations, and hardware states to establish absolute timing guarantees. Modern embedded systems engineering approaches integrate WCET analysis early in the development cycle to identify potential timing issues before they become critical problems. The consequences of inadequate timing analysis extend beyond safety concerns. Embedded applications face unique challenges that make timing analysis particularly complex. The increasing complexity of embedded processors, with features like multi-level caches, branch prediction, and out-of-order execution, makes timing behaviour less predictable. Modern processor architectures present significant challenges for **timing analysis**. Branch prediction mechanisms, designed to improve average performance, introduce timing variability that complicates WCET analysis. These tools typically integrate with development environments and provide detailed timing reports, including execution path analysis and bottleneck identification. The analysis should be automated as part of the build process, with timing budgets established early in the design phase. Continuous integration systems can automatically run WCET analysis and flag potential timing violations. Best practices for startups implementing timing analysis include:. * Training development teams on timing analysis principles. * Collaborating with timing analysis experts for complex projects. The key to successful implementation lies in understanding that WCET analysis is not a one-time activity but an ongoing process throughout the development lifecycle. For growing companies developing embedded systems and IoT solutions, investing in proper timing analysis capabilities provides a competitive advantage through improved product reliability and faster time-to-market. Understanding and implementing WCET analysis ensures that your real-time systems will meet their timing requirements, providing the foundation for successful and safe embedded applications.

Methods for Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) analysis have been known for some time, and recently commercial tools have emerged. Here, we present a case study where static WCET analysis was used to find upper time bounds for time-critical regions in a commercial real-time operating system. In this article, we present a casestudy where static Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) analysiswas used to find upper time bounds for time-critical code inproducts from Volcano Communications Technologies AB (VCT).The VCT company provides tools for development of real-timecommunication solutions for embedded network systems, mainlyused within the car industry. Static Worst Case Execution Time (WCET) analysis is a technique that computes an upper bound of the execution time of a program before runtime. Static WCET analysis has a potential to cut costs and save time in the development of real-time systems. The main goal of this thesis work was to bring static WCET analysis into the education of new real-time systems developers, thereby making them aware of the benefits of WCET analysis tools.

Title: Mollie McGill – We Will Miss You - WCET
# Mollie McGill – We Will Miss You. Published by: WCET | 1/7/2021. On December 31, 2020, our beloved Mollie McGill ended 32 years of serving WICHE, WCET, and their members. This post highlights fond reminiscences, well-deserved honors for Mollie, and a new honor for her. ## **Mollie and the Pre-WCET Years**. At WICHE, Mollie worked successfully on several projects and was elevated to the role of executive assistant to the WICHE executive director, as the leader was then titled. WICHE’s deputy director, Dick Jonsen, picked Mollie to help develop (what was originally called) the Western Regional Telecommunications Cooperative. In 1987 – 89, Mollie and Dick traveled to each state to conduct meetings to ascertain the viability of such an organization. Not only did David serve on the first WCET Steering Committee, but he also recalled how he, Mollie, and Charlotte Farr led the dancing contingent at Annual Meetings. Sally and Mollie invited me to come be the fourth staff member with Dale Cracraft (running meetings and operations….and a character in her own right) being the third. Working with Sally and Mollie on something new was very enticing. Of course, she went there to demonstrate her excellence and was named “Administrator of the Year.” Meanwhile, Mollie and I would stay in touch and would sometimes have lunch at Carelli’s in Boulder. news brief with text: at its may 4 meeting, faculty council gave its administrator of the year award to mollie mcgill, CU director of learning innovations and tech, and Rick Forsman director of .... 32 years at WICHE and WCET*. We asked Dick Jonsen if he would be willing to share billing with Mollie, just as he shared time traveling with her to every WICHE state so many years ago. **Dick Jonsen & Mollie McGill Award**. We have created a padlet for everyone to share their memories of Mollie and to wish her well in retirement.
